extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory set theory and proof techniques (e.g., in a 'transition to proofs' course)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapter explaining basic set notions (Cartesian product, subsets, power sets, set operations, complements, Venn diagrams, indexed sets) with examples and exercises for undergraduate proof students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product / Cartesian power
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A and B, A × B is the set of ordered pairs (a,b) with a∈A and b∈B. The Cartesian power A^n (or S^7) denotes n-tuples; e.g., S^7 describes possible outcomes of seven coin tosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two-by-three matrices with real entries are arrangements of six reals but are not the same thing as elements of R^6 (M ≠ R^6). For a set S with |S|=2 (coin sides {h,t}), |S^7| = 2^7 = 128. Use Cartesian product to form sets of ordered tuples and reason about their cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of subset (A ⊆ B) and non-subset (A ⊄ B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ B iff every element of A is also an element of B. We write A ⊄ B to mean it is not true that every element of A is in B (i.e., there exists an element of A not in B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and checks: list elements to test subset relations; note that A ⊆ A for any set A. The text uses many worked examples to illustrate membership vs subset (e.g., {1,3} ⊆ B vs {1,3} ∈ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty set is a subset of every set
rubrics_metrics.description: The empty set ∅ is a subset of every set B, i.e., ∅ ⊆ B for any set B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: ∅ ⊄ B would require an element of ∅ not in B, which is impossible because ∅ has no elements. Examples illustrate how ∅ can both be an element of a set (∅ ∈ {∅}) and a subset (∅ ⊆ X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing subsets via branching/tree method and cardinality doubling
rubrics_metrics.description: To list all subsets of a finite set B, build a binary branching tree deciding for each element whether to include it; at each branching the number of subsets doubles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For B={a,b,c} the tree yields 8 subsets. Fact: If a finite set has n elements then it has 2^n subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set P(A) definition and cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: P(A) is the set of all subsets of A: P(A) = { X : X ⊆ A } .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A is finite with |A|=n then |P(A)| = 2^n. Examples: explicit listing for small finite A; warnings: P(1) is meaningless because 1 is not a set. For infinite A, P(A) is usually not listable and can be extremely large (e.g., P(R^2) contains every imaginable subset of the plane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set operations: union, intersection, difference (definitions and basic properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: A ∪ B = { x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B }. A ∩ B = { x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B }. A − B = { x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In words: union = elements in A or B (or both); intersection = elements in both; difference = elements in A but not in B. Properties: ∪ and ∩ are commutative (X ∪ Y = Y ∪ X, X ∩ Y = Y ∩ X). In general, A − B ≠ B − A. Numerous worked examples (finite lists, intervals, Cartesian products, graphs) illustrate these definitions and operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement relative to a universal set
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a universal set U containing A, the complement A (written A with an overbar in text) is A = U − A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a natural universal set for context (e.g., primes P ⊆ Z; graphs ⊆ R^2). Examples show complements as 'everything in the universe that is not in A' (e.g., primes complement = composites ∪ {1}). Exercises use specified U to compute complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venn diagrams as visualization tools and parentheses rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Venn diagrams represent sets as regions (circles/ovals) inside a universe and help visualize unions/intersections/differences; they are informal scratch-work devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important points given: if an expression uses only ∪, parentheses are optional; if only ∩, parentheses are optional; if an expression uses both ∪ and ∩, parentheses are essential (e.g., A ∪ B ∩ C is ambiguous without parentheses). Use diagrams to compare expressions and test identities (examples: shading for A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A − B, and three-set diagrams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed sets and big-union / big-intersection notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a collection of sets {A_i : i ∈ I}, define ⋃_{i∈I} A_i = { x : x ∈ A_i for at least one i∈I } and ⋂_{i∈I} A_i = { x : x ∈ A_i for every i∈I }. Index set I may be finite, infinite, integers, reals, or any set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation analogues to sigma notation are introduced: ∑ vs ⋃/⋂. Examples: finite unions/intersections, infinite unions (⋃_{i=1}^∞ A_i) and parameterized families A_α for α∈I (e.g., rectangles A_α = [α,2]×[0,α] for α∈[0,2]). Show how index sets need not be integers and how to use set-of-indices notation (⋃_{i∈{1,2,3}} A_i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical objects by type (tuples vs structured objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although different constructions may have the same underlying list of entries (e.g., a 2×3 matrix and a 6-tuple of real numbers), they are considered different mathematical objects: M ≠ R^6 in the sense that two-by-three matrices are not the same things as sequences of six numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to respect the intended structure when identifying sets: even if elements correspond coordinatewise, their interpretations/meanings and operations may differ. The textbook emphasizes maintaining distinction between arrangements and tuples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality facts for products and power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardinality of Cartesian powers and power sets: for finite sets A and B with |A|=m, |B|=n, |A×B| = m·n; for Cartesian power S^n, |S^n| = |S|^n; for finite A, |P(A)| = 2^{|A|}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask for cardinalities like |P(A×B)|, |P(A)×P(B)|, |P(P(A))|, etc. Use these identities to compute sizes of constructed sets; examples and problems reinforce counting arguments (e.g., listing outcomes, tree-doubling).
